lessons.title: tenga, diga, quiera — old irregularities come free
lessons.gloss: irregular yo stems and stressed stem changes carry into the subjunctive automatically

segments.text: The subjunctive recipe begins with the present yo form. That means irregular stems you already know travel into the new mood with you.
Drop the final -o, keep the g, and add the opposite-vowel endings:

utterances: verb: tener. yo form: tengo. subjunctive: tenga.
verb: decir. yo form: digo. subjunctive: diga.
verb: hacer. yo form: hago. subjunctive: haga.
verb: poner. yo form: pongo. subjunctive: ponga.
verb: salir. yo form: salgo. subjunctive: salga.
verb: venir. yo form: vengo. subjunctive: venga.

segments.text: Six irregular verbs require no new irregular stem.
Chapter 11's stressed changes also carry over:

utterances: verb: querer. yo form: quiero. subjunctive: quiera.
verb: poder. yo form: puedo. subjunctive: pueda.

segments.text: The nosotros forms keep the plain stem: queramos, podamos, not quieramos or puedamos. As in the indicative, the stress has moved away from the stem, so the diphthong disappears.

segments.instruction: "tengo becomes tenga; digo becomes diga; hago becomes haga"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "tengo → tenga; digo → diga; hago → haga"]

segments.instruction: "pongo becomes ponga; salgo becomes salga; vengo becomes venga"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "pongo → ponga; salgo → salga; vengo → venga"]

segments.text: Why does tenga keep its g? (It comes from tengo.) How many new stems does the -go club require? (Zero.) Why are queramos and podamos plain? (The stem is unstressed in nosotros.)

lessons.title: ojalá — a wish borrowed whole
lessons.gloss: a wish-word borrowed from Andalusi Arabic that triggers the subjunctive without que or a main verb

segments.text: Ojalá hable español. — I hope he speaks Spanish. / May he speak Spanish.
Ojalá takes the subjunctive without que or a separate main verb. The word itself expresses the wish, so there is no factual assertion to put in the indicative.
The standard account derives ojalá from Andalusi Arabic law šāʾ Allāh, "if God should will." The Allāh remains audible in the second half.

Chapter 5 gave you another Arabic function word: hasta, from ḥattā. Borrowing nouns such as azúcar, aceite, and álgebra is ordinary. Borrowing grammatical tools is rarer. Spanish borrowed both a preposition and a word that selects a whole mood.
English "God willing" expresses the same idea, and English has now borrowed Arabic inshallah directly as well.

segments.source: [YOU SAY: "ojalá venga" — I hope she comes]
[YOU SAY: "hasta / ojalá" — two Arabic function words]

segments.text: Does ojalá require que? (No.) Which mood follows it? (The subjunctive.) What is its source phrase? (Andalusi Arabic law šāʾ Allāh, "if God should will.") Which other Arabic function word have you learned? (Hasta.)

lessons.title: Chapter 18 practice — fact or wish?
lessons.gloss: drilling the vowel flip and inherited stems

segments.text: Two skills to drill, in order: build the form, then decide whether you need it.
Give the yo subjunctive. Recipe: yo form becomes drop -o becomes flip the vowel.

utterances: verb: hablar. yo form: hablo. becomes subjunctive: hable.
verb: estudiar. yo form: estudio. becomes subjunctive: estudie.
verb: comer. yo form: como. becomes subjunctive: coma.
verb: beber. yo form: bebo. becomes subjunctive: beba.
verb: vivir. yo form: vivo. becomes subjunctive: viva.
verb: tener. yo form: tengo. becomes subjunctive: tenga.
verb: hacer. yo form: hago. becomes subjunctive: haga.
verb: venir. yo form: vengo. becomes subjunctive: venga.
verb: querer. yo form: quiero. becomes subjunctive: quiera.
verb: poder. yo form: puedo. becomes subjunctive: pueda.

segments.text: The last four are the point: you never learned a new stem. The -go and the diphthong were already in the yo form.
Then the four with no -o to strip, which you learn outright: ser becomes sea, ir becomes vaya, saber becomes sepa, haber becomes haya.

And estar, which looks like it belongs with them and doesn't: estoy has no strippable -o either, but take off the whole -oy and the stem est- is completely ordinary — esté, estés, esté, estemos, estén.

Its oddity is stress, not spelling. Spanish stresses the second-to-last syllable of a word ending in a vowel, -n or -s — hablar obeys that throughout (HA-ble, ha-BLE-mos, HA-blen). Estar doesn't: es-TÉ, es-TÉS, es-TÉN all land on the last syllable, so each needs a written accent. Only es-TE-mos falls where Spanish expects, and it takes none.

Recite the recipe. (Yo form, drop the -o, flip the vowel.) Which earlier irregulars come along free? (The -go club of Ch. 12–13 and Ch. 11's stem-changers.) What's the two-subject test? (If the second verb has Ch. 11's stem-changers.) Which yo forms leave no -o to strip, and which of them is still predictable? (Soy, voy, sé, he, estoy — and estoy is the predictable one, est- + normal endings.) Where does estar's irregularity actually live? (In the stress — es-TÉ lands on the last syllable, breaking Spanish's second-to-last default, which is what the accent records.)

lessons.title: Practice — fact or wish?
lessons.gloss: choosing indicative versus subjunctive and hearing the opposite-vowel contrast

segments.text: Report the world with the indicative; reach for a different world with the subjunctive.

utterances: Sé que comes aquí., I know you eat here. (fact).
Quiero que comas aquí., I want you to eat here. (wish).
Sé que está aquí., I know he is here. (fact).
Ojalá esté aquí., I hope he is here. (wish).
Dice que viene., She says she is coming. (report).
Quiero que venga., I want her to come. (wish).

segments.text: Ojalá needs no que and no main verb. It is the wish.

utterances: indicative: habla. subjunctive: hable.
indicative: come. subjunctive: coma.
indicative: trabaja. subjunctive: trabaje.
indicative: vive. subjunctive: viva.

segments.text: Also distinguish hable from hablé, and trabaje from trabajé. The written accent separates present subjunctive from "I" preterite.

segments.source: [YOU SAY: "sé que comes / quiero que comas"]
[YOU SAY: "dice que viene / quiero que venga"]

segments.text: Why is sé que comes indicative? (It reports a fact.) What does ojalá need before its subjunctive? (Nothing.) What does the accent distinguish in hable/hablé? (Present subjunctive from first-person preterite.)

lessons.title: Practice — one subject or two?
lessons.gloss: choosing infinitive versus que plus subjunctive after wanting

segments.text: Does the second verb have a different subject?

utterances: I want to eat., Quiero comer. (same becomes infinitive).
I want you to eat., Quiero que comas. (two becomes clause).
We want to live here., Queremos vivir aquí.
We want them to live here., Queremos que vivan aquí.
She wants to work., Quiere trabajar.
She wants me to work., Quiere que yo trabaje.

segments.text: Say each pair back to back. English changes quietly from "to eat" to "you to eat." Spanish marks the new subject with que and a conjugated verb.

segments.source: [YOU SAY: "quiere trabajar / quiere que yo trabaje"]

segments.text: Same subject after querer: which form? (Infinitive.) Different subject? (Que + subjunctive.) Translate "I want to eat" and "I want you to eat." (Quiero comer / Quiero que comas.)

lessons.title: quiero que… — making the subjunctive appear
lessons.gloss: what triggers the subjunctive — one subject wanting another to act

segments.text: You can now build the subjunctive. This lesson is about what makes it show up — and the core case is beautifully simple: one person wanting a different person to do something.
Compare:

utterances: Quiero hablar español., I want to speak Spanish.
Quiero que hables español., I want you to speak Spanish.

segments.text: The first has one subject — I want, I speak — so Spanish uses a plain infinitive, exactly like English.
The second has two. I am the wanter; you are the speaker. The moment the subjects differ, Spanish must:
join the halves with que, and.
put the second verb in the subjunctive.
Quiero que hables. — Two subjects, so que, so subjunctive.
That is the subiūnctīvus of last lesson doing exactly what its name says: living in a clause joined underneath the main one.
Hables is not a report that you speak. It's what I want — which may never happen. The main clause reaches out and bends the second one into something unreal, and the mood marks the bend.
Watch the difference this makes:

utterances: Sé que hablas español., I know that you speak Spanish. (a fact — indicative).
Quiero que hables español., I want you to speak Spanish. (not yet real — subjunctive).

segments.text: Same que, same person, different mood — because knowing reports the world and wanting tries to change it.

segments.instruction: the two-subject version — "Quiero que hables español"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the two-subject version — "Quiero **que hables** español"]

segments.instruction: the contrast — "Sé que hablas … quiero que hables"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the contrast — "Sé que **hablas** … quiero que **hables**"]

segments.text: What makes the subjunctive appear after querer? (Two different subjects — joined by que.) Say "I want to speak" and "I want you to speak." (Quiero hablar / Quiero que hables.) Why does Sé que hablas stay indicative? (Knowing reports a fact; wanting doesn't.) What joins the two subjects? (Que, followed by the subjunctive.)

lessons.title: subjuntivo — "joined underneath"
lessons.gloss: joined underneath — a mood named for its grammatical position in a subordinate clause

segments.text: Latin subiūnctīvus means "joined underneath": sub- (under) + iungere (join). English join, junction, and conjunction descend from that Latin verb.
English yoke and Sanskrit yoga are cousins rather than descendants. All three branches reach Proto-Indo-European yewg-, "join": a yoke joins oxen; yoga names a yoking; a conjunction joins clauses.

Latin's term translated Greek hypotaktikḗ, "subordinated." The name describes where the mood lives: in a clause hanging under a main clause. It does not claim that every subjunctive sentence has one single meaning.

What does subjunctive literally mean? (Joined underneath.) Which English words descend from iungere? (Join, junction, conjunction.) Which two are older cousins? (Yoke and yoga.) What does the name describe? (The mood's grammatical position.)

lessons.title: sea, vaya, sepa, haya; esté — where the shortcut stops
lessons.gloss: four forms must be learned outright, while estar keeps a regular stem with exceptional stress

segments.text: The drop-o recipe cannot start from soy, voy, sé, he:

utterances: verb: ser. yo form: soy. subjunctive: sea.
verb: ir. yo form: voy. subjunctive: vaya.
verb: saber. yo form: sé. subjunctive: sepa.
verb: haber. yo form: he. subjunctive: haya.

segments.text: Learn those four. Sea also recalls a fact from Chapter 9: forms of Latin sedēre, "to sit," joined the history of ser. It descends from Latin sedeam.
Remove all of -oy from estoy and the ordinary stem est- remains: esté, estés, esté, estemos, estén.
The accents record final stress that breaks Spanish's default:
es-TÉ, es-TÉS, es-TÉN — accent required.
es-TE-mos — default second-to-last stress, no accent.
Dar similarly shrinks doy to d-: dé, des, dé, demos, den. The accent on one-syllable dé distinguishes the verb from preposition de; it does not move stress.
Treat "no -o to strip" as a modern memory aid, not a historical cause. Sea, vaya, sepa, haya descend from Latin sedeam, vādam, sapiam, habeam.

segments.source: [YOU SAY: "dé" the verb versus "de" the preposition]

segments.text: Which four forms are learned outright? (Sea, vaya, sepa, haya.) What is regular about estar? (Its est- stem and endings.) Why does esté need an accent but estemos does not? (Final stress breaks the default; second-to-last stress obeys it.)

lessons.title: hable, coma, viva — the subjunctive
lessons.gloss: the regular present subjunctive — built from the yo form, with the vowel flipped

needs: your eyes for one table that cannot be read aloud
waitUntilStopped: Building it: take the yo form and flip the vowel
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes for one table that cannot be read aloud. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called Building it: take the yo form and flip the vowel until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Every tense so far — hablo, hablé, hablaba, hablaré, hablaría — has belonged to one mood, the indicative: the mood of assertion. It states how things are, and it keeps stating even when it guesses (Chapter 17's Serán las tres, "it must be three," is still an assertion — a confident one about an unknown).

Spanish has another mood for what is not asserted at all: things wanted, doubted, feared, hoped for. That is the subjunctive, and the good news is that you have already learned most of it without knowing.

blocks.title: Building it: take the yo form and flip the vowel

segments.text: Not from the infinitive. From the yo form of the present.
Take the yo form: hablo, como, vivo.
Drop the -o: habl-, com-, viv-.
Add the opposite vowel.
"Opposite" is the whole trick:

utterances: verb type: -ar. present takes…: -a- (hablas). subjunctive takes…: -e- (hables).
verb type: -er / -ir. present takes…: -e- / -i- (comes). subjunctive takes…: -a- (comas).

segments.text: The two families swap costumes.

There is a table here I cannot read to you — 4 columns and 5 rows, and it has more columns than can be held in the ear at once. Its columns are: one with no heading, hablar, comer, vivir. Come back and look at it when you have stopped.
Note -er and -ir are identical here — as they already were in the Ch. 15 preterite and the Ch. 16 imperfect. Outside the present tense, those two conjugations keep merging.

segments.instruction: the recipe — "yo form, drop the -o, flip the vowel"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the recipe — "**yo** form, drop the **-o**, **flip the vowel**"]

segments.text: What do you build the subjunctive from? (The yo form of the present — not the infinitive.) What happens to the vowel? (It flips: -ar verbs take -e, -er/-ir take -a.) Give comer. (Coma, comas, coma, comamos, coman.) What happens to the -go club? (It transfers whole — tenga, diga, haga, ponga, salga, venga; the next step makes that inheritance explicit.)

lessons.title: quiero que hables — do not smuggle in a subject
lessons.gloss: Spanish requires a full clause for a second subject after wanting, but permits object plus infinitive with perception and causation

segments.text: English says "I want you to speak": an object plus an infinitive. Spanish will not copy that shape after a verb of wanting. There is no quiero te hablar with that meaning. Use a full clause:
Quiero que hables. — I want you to speak.
The rule belongs to volition, not to every Spanish verb. Object plus infinitive works after perception and causation:
Te vi salir. — I saw you leave.
Me hizo hablar. — He made me speak.
Déjame hablar. — Let me speak.

And quiero hablarte is valid: "I want to speak to you." It still has one subject—I want and I speak—and te is the object of speaking. What fails is using a pronoun to introduce a second doer after querer.

segments.instruction: "quiero hablarte" — I want to speak to you
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "quiero hablarte" — I want to speak to you]

segments.instruction: "quiero que hables" — I want you to speak
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "quiero que hables" — I want you to speak]

segments.instruction: "te vi salir" — perception allows object + infinitive
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "te vi salir" — perception allows object + infinitive]

segments.text: How does Spanish say "I want you to speak"? (Quiero que hables.) Why is quiero hablarte different? (It has one subject; te is an object.) Name one verb family that permits object plus infinitive. (Perception or causation.)
